Previously... ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1|3-6|8-10|"} library(tidymodels) set.seed(123) cls_split <- initial_split(cls_data_2026, prop = 0.8) cls_train <- training(cls_split) cls_test <- testing(cls_split) tree_spec <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0.0001, mode = "classification") cls_wflow <- workflow(class ~ ., tree_spec) cls_fit <- fit(cls_wflow, cls_train) ``` ::: ## A logistic regression fit ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1-3|5|16|"} lr_fit <- logistic_reg() |> fit(class ~ ., data = cls_train) augment(lr_fit, new_data = cls_train) |> print(n = 5) #> # A tibble: 800 × 6 #> .pred_class .pred_class_1 .pred_class_2 pred_1 pred_2 class #> #> 1 class_1 0.832 0.168 -1.35 -0.446 class_1 #> 2 class_1 0.892 0.108 -0.354 -0.181 class_1 #> 3 class_2 0.0434 0.957 0.105 1.12 class_2 #> 4 class_1 0.999 0.000548 0.0203 -1.20 class_1 #> 5 class_1 0.963 0.0373 -0.831 -0.607 class_1 #> # ℹ 795 more rows lr_re_pred <- augment(lr_fit, new_data = cls_train) ``` ::: ## Confusion matrix ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ![](images/confusion-matrix.png) ## Confusion matrix ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_re_pred |> conf_mat(truth = class, estimate = .pred_class) #> Truth #> Prediction class_1 class_2 #> class_1 500 36 #> class_2 34 230 ``` ::: ## Confusion matrix ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_re_pred |> conf_mat(truth = class, estimate = .pred_class) |> autoplot(type = "heatmap") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](figures/conf-mat-plot-1.svg){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ## Metrics for model performance ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: columns ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_re_pred |> accuracy(truth = class, estimate = .pred_class) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 accuracy binary 0.912 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](images/confusion-matrix-accuracy.png) ::: ::: ::: {.absolute bottom=0 right=0} [AML4TD](https://aml4td.org/chapters/cls-metrics.html#sec-cls-hard-metrics) ::: ## Dangers of accuracy ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} We need to be careful of using `accuracy()` since it can give "good" performance by only predicting one way with imbalanced data: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1|2|3|"} lr_re_pred |> mutate(.pred_class = factor("class_1", levels = c("class_1", "class_2"))) |> accuracy(truth = class, estimate = .pred_class) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 accuracy binary 0.668 ``` ::: ## Brier score formula What if we don't turn predicted probabilities into class predictions? . . . The Brier score is analogous to the mean squared error in regression models: $$ Brier = \frac{1}{NC}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{k=1}^C (y_{ik} - \hat{p}_{ik})^2 $$ ::: {.absolute bottom=0 right=0} [AML4TD](https://aml4td.org/chapters/cls-metrics.html#sec-brier) ::: ## Brier score {.annotation} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_re_pred |> brier_class(truth = class, .pred_class_1) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 brier_class binary 0.0665 ``` ::: . . . Smaller values are better. . . .
For binary classification: - The "bad model threshold" is about 0.25. - A single column is given for the probability estimates (unnamed). ## Separation and calibration ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} Accuracy measures separation. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](figures/separation-example-1.svg){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} The Brier score captures calibration. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](figures/calibration-example-1.svg){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.absolute bottom=0 right=0} [AML4TD](https://aml4td.org/chapters/cls-metrics.html#sec-metric-information) ::: ::: notes - Good separation: the densities don't overlap. - Good calibration: the calibration line follows the diagonal. Calibration plot: We bin observations according to predicted probability. In the bin for 20%-30% predicted prob, we should see an event rate of ~25% if the model is well-calibrated. ::: ## Separation and (bad) calibration ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} Excellent separation ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](figures/bad-separation-example-1.svg){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} Terrible calibration. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](figures/bad-calibration-example-1.svg){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Your turn {transition="slide-in"} ![](images/parsnip-flagger.jpg){.absolute top="0" right="0" width="150" height="150"} The probably package was used to make the calibration plots: ```r library(probably) lr_re_pred |> cal_plot_breaks(class, .pred_class_1) ```
Try the other calibration curve methods in probably: - [`cal_plot_logistic()`](https://probably.tidymodels.org/reference/cal_plot_logistic.html) - [`cal_plot_windowed()`](https://probably.tidymodels.org/reference/cal_plot_windowed.html) Do you prefer one over the others? ::: {.cell} ::: ## Metrics for model performance ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} We can use `metric_set()` to combine multiple calculations into one ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cls_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, brier_class) lr_re_pred |> cls_metrics(truth = class, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_class_1) #> # A tibble: 2 × 3 #> .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 accuracy binary 0.912 #> 2 brier_class binary 0.0665 ``` ::: ## Metrics for model performance ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} Metrics and metric sets work with grouped data frames! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_re_pred |> mutate(group = rep_len(LETTERS[1:3], nrow(cls_train))) |> group_by(group) |> cls_metrics(truth = class, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_class_1) #> # A tibble: 6 × 4 #> group .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 A accuracy binary 0.899 #> 2 B accuracy binary 0.906 #> 3 C accuracy binary 0.932 #> 4 A brier_class binary 0.0689 #> 5 B brier_class binary 0.0693 #> 6 C brier_class binary 0.0613 ``` ::: ## {background-iframe="https://yardstick.tidymodels.org/reference/index.html"} ::: footer ::: # ⚠️ DANGERS OF OVERFITTING ⚠️ ## Dangers of overfitting ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](figures/overfitting-training-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ::: {.absolute bottom=0 right=0} [AML4TD](https://aml4td.org/chapters/overfitting.html) ::: ## Dangers of overfitting ⚠️ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](figures/overfitting-testing-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ## Dangers of overfitting - The underfit model's performance didn't change that much. It is too simple and can't overfit - The overfit model is too complex: - It is chasing specific data points so that it can predict the training set points as perfectly as possible. - It _over_ adapts to the training data because it can be very flexible. - We can't really know if it under- or overfits until we have different data for model _fitting_ and model _evaluation_. ## Dangers of overfitting ⚠️ ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_fit |> augment(cls_train) |> print(n = 5) #> # A tibble: 800 × 6 #> .pred_class .pred_class_1 .pred_class_2 pred_1 pred_2 class #> #> 1 class_1 0.832 0.168 -1.35 -0.446 class_1 #> 2 class_1 0.892 0.108 -0.354 -0.181 class_1 #> 3 class_2 0.0434 0.957 0.105 1.12 class_2 #> 4 class_1 0.999 0.000548 0.0203 -1.20 class_1 #> 5 class_1 0.963 0.0373 -0.831 -0.607 class_1 #> # ℹ 795 more rows ``` :::
We call this "resubstitution" or "repredicting the training set" ## Dangers of overfitting ⚠️ ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_fit |> augment(cls_train) |> accuracy(class, .pred_class) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 accuracy binary 0.912 ``` ::: We call this a "resubstitution estimate" ## Dangers of overfitting ⚠️ ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_fit |> augment(cls_train) |> accuracy(class, .pred_class) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 accuracy binary 0.912 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: ::: ## Dangers of overfitting ⚠️ ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_fit |> augment(cls_train) |> accuracy(class, .pred_class) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 accuracy binary 0.912 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_fit |> augment(cls_test) |> accuracy(class, .pred_class) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 accuracy binary 0.895 ``` ::: ::: ::: . . . Why aren't the numbers very different? . . . Can basic logistic regression overfit? . . . ⚠️ Remember that we're demonstrating overfitting . . . ⚠️ Don't use the test set until the *end* of your modeling analysis ## {background-image="https://media.giphy.com/media/55itGuoAJiZEEen9gg/giphy.gif" background-size="70%"} ## Dangers of overfitting ⚠️ ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_fit |> augment(cls_train) |> brier_class(class, .pred_class_1) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 brier_class binary 0.0665 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_fit |> augment(cls_test) |> brier_class(class, .pred_class_1) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 brier_class binary 0.0736 ``` ::: ::: ::: . . . What if we want to compare more models? . . . And/or more model configurations? . . . And we want to understand if these are important differences? # The testing data are precious 💎 # How can we use the *training* data to compare and evaluate different models? 🤔 ## {background-color="white" background-image="https://www.tmwr.org/premade/resampling.svg" background-size="80%"} ## Cross-validation ![](https://www.tmwr.org/premade/three-CV.svg) ::: {.absolute bottom=0 right=0} [AML4TD](https://aml4td.org/chapters/resampling.html#sec-cv) ::: ## Cross-validation ![](https://www.tmwr.org/premade/three-CV-iter.svg) ## Your turn {transition="slide-in"} ![](images/parsnip-flagger.jpg){.absolute top="0" right="0" width="150" height="150"} *If we use 10 folds, what percent of the training data* - *ends up in analysis* - *ends up in assessment* ::: {.cell} ::: ## Cross-validation ![](hexes/rsample.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vfold_cv(cls_train) # v = 10 is default #> # 10-fold cross-validation #> # A tibble: 10 × 2 #> splits id #> #> 1 Fold01 #> 2 Fold02 #> 3 Fold03 #> 4 Fold04 #> 5 Fold05 #> 6 Fold06 #> 7 Fold07 #> 8 Fold08 #> 9 Fold09 #> 10 Fold10 ``` ::: ## Cross-validation ![](hexes/rsample.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} What is in this? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cls_folds <- vfold_cv(cls_train) cls_folds$splits[1:3] #> [[1]] #> #> <720/80/800> #> #> [[2]] #> #> <720/80/800> #> #> [[3]] #> #> <720/80/800> ``` ::: ::: notes Talk about a list column, storing non-atomic types in dataframe ::: ## Cross-validation ![](hexes/rsample.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vfold_cv(cls_train, v = 5) #> # 5-fold cross-validation #> # A tibble: 5 × 2 #> splits id #> #> 1 Fold1 #> 2 Fold2 #> 3 Fold3 #> 4 Fold4 #> 5 Fold5 ``` ::: ## Cross-validation ![](hexes/rsample.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} We'll use this setup: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(343) cls_folds <- vfold_cv(cls_train, v = 10) cls_folds #> # 10-fold cross-validation #> # A tibble: 10 × 2 #> splits id #> #> 1 Fold01 #> 2 Fold02 #> 3 Fold03 #> 4 Fold04 #> 5 Fold05 #> 6 Fold06 #> 7 Fold07 #> 8 Fold08 #> 9 Fold09 #> 10 Fold10 ``` ::: . . . Set the seed when creating resamples # We are equipped with metrics and resamples! ## Fit our model to the resamples ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1|3|4|"} lr_wflow <- workflow(class ~ ., logistic_reg()) cls_res <- fit_resamples(lr_wflow, cls_folds) cls_res #> # Resampling results #> # 10-fold cross-validation #> # A tibble: 10 × 4 #> splits id .metrics .notes #> #> 1 Fold01 #> 2 Fold02 #> 3 Fold03 #> 4 Fold04 #> 5 Fold05 #> 6 Fold06 #> 7 Fold07 #> 8 Fold08 #> 9 Fold09 #> 10 Fold10 ``` ::: ## Evaluating model performance ![](hexes/tune.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cls_res |> collect_metrics() #> # A tibble: 3 × 6 #> .metric .estimator mean n std_err .config #> #> 1 accuracy binary 0.911 10 0.0124 pre0_mod0_post0 #> 2 brier_class binary 0.0680 10 0.00663 pre0_mod0_post0 #> 3 roc_auc binary 0.966 10 0.00505 pre0_mod0_post0 ``` ::: ::: notes `collect_metrics()` is one of a suite of `collect_*()` functions that can be used to work with columns of tuning results. Most columns in a tuning result prefixed with `.` have a corresponding `collect_*()` function with options for common summaries. ::: . . . We can reliably measure performance using only the **training** data 🎉 ## Comparing metrics ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} How do the metrics from resampling compare to the metrics from training and testing? ::: {.cell} ::: ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cls_res |> collect_metrics() |> select(.metric, mean, std_err, n) #> # A tibble: 3 × 4 #> .metric mean std_err n #> #> 1 accuracy 0.911 0.0124 10 #> 2 brier_class 0.0680 0.00663 10 #> 3 roc_auc 0.966 0.00505 10 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} The Brier score previously was - 0.067 for the training set - 0.074 for test set ::: ::: . . . Remember that: ⚠️ the training set gives you overly optimistic metrics ⚠️ the test set is precious ## Your turn {transition="slide-in"} ![](images/parsnip-flagger.jpg){.absolute top="0" right="0" width="150" height="150"}
Rerun the same code three times with different random number seeds. How much do the results change? ::: {.cell} ::: ## Evaluating model performance ![](hexes/tune.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1-2|3|5|"} # Save the assessment set results ctrl_rs <- control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE) cls_res <- fit_resamples(lr_wflow, cls_folds, control = ctrl_rs) cls_res #> # Resampling results #> # 10-fold cross-validation #> # A tibble: 10 × 5 #> splits id .metrics .notes .predictions #> #> 1 Fold01 #> 2 Fold02 #> 3 Fold03 #> 4 Fold04 #> 5 Fold05 #> 6 Fold06 #> 7 Fold07 #> 8 Fold08 #> 9 Fold09 #> 10 Fold10 ``` ::: ## Evaluating model performance ![](hexes/tune.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ![](hexes/probably.png){.absolute top=-20 right=64 width="64" height="74.24"} probably has a nice interface for calibration curves: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(probably) cal_plot_windowed(cls_res, step_size = 0.03) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](figures/fit-resamples-cal-plot-1.svg) ::: :::
The out-of-sample predictions are pooled before computing the calibration curve. ## Evaluating model performance ![](hexes/tune.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Save the assessment set results cls_preds <- collect_predictions(cls_res) cls_preds |> slice(1:5) #> # A tibble: 5 × 7 #> .pred_class .pred_class_1 .pred_class_2 id class .row .config #> #> 1 class_1 1.000 0.000371 Fold01 class_1 14 pre0_mod0_post0 #> 2 class_2 0.267 0.733 Fold01 class_1 24 pre0_mod0_post0 #> 3 class_1 0.997 0.00253 Fold01 class_1 32 pre0_mod0_post0 #> 4 class_1 0.748 0.252 Fold01 class_1 41 pre0_mod0_post0 #> 5 class_1 1.000 0.000323 Fold01 class_1 42 pre0_mod0_post0 ``` ::: ## Evaluating model performance ![](hexes/tune.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cls_preds |> group_by(id) |> cls_metrics(truth = class, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_class_1) #> # A tibble: 20 × 4 #> id .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 Fold01 accuracy binary 0.862 #> 2 Fold02 accuracy binary 0.85 #> 3 Fold03 accuracy binary 0.988 #> 4 Fold04 accuracy binary 0.925 #> 5 Fold05 accuracy binary 0.888 #> 6 Fold06 accuracy binary 0.925 #> 7 Fold07 accuracy binary 0.925 #> 8 Fold08 accuracy binary 0.938 #> 9 Fold09 accuracy binary 0.912 #> 10 Fold10 accuracy binary 0.9 #> 11 Fold01 brier_class binary 0.0891 #> 12 Fold02 brier_class binary 0.0908 #> 13 Fold03 brier_class binary 0.0245 #> 14 Fold04 brier_class binary 0.0647 #> 15 Fold05 brier_class binary 0.0974 #> 16 Fold06 brier_class binary 0.0588 #> 17 Fold07 brier_class binary 0.0573 #> 18 Fold08 brier_class binary 0.0659 #> 19 Fold09 brier_class binary 0.0634 #> 20 Fold10 brier_class binary 0.0678 ``` ::: ## Where are the fitted models? ![](hexes/tune.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} {.annotation} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cls_res #> # Resampling results #> # 10-fold cross-validation #> # A tibble: 10 × 5 #> splits id .metrics .notes .predictions #> #> 1 Fold01 #> 2 Fold02 #> 3 Fold03 #> 4 Fold04 #> 5 Fold05 #> 6 Fold06 #> 7 Fold07 #> 8 Fold08 #> 9 Fold09 #> 10 Fold10 ``` ::: . . . 🗑️ ## The whole game - status update ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](images/whole-game-transparent-resamples.jpg){fig-align='center' width=3543} ::: ::: # Backup Slides {background-color="#BDE9C9FF"} ## Metrics for model performance ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: columns ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_re_pred |> sensitivity(truth = class, estimate = .pred_class) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 sensitivity binary 0.936 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](images/confusion-matrix-sensitivity.png) ::: ::: ::: {.absolute bottom=0 left=0} [AML4TD](https://aml4td.org/chapters/cls-metrics.html#sec-cls-two-classes) ::: ## Metrics for model performance ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: columns ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="3-6"} lr_re_pred |> sensitivity(truth = class, estimate = .pred_class) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 sensitivity binary 0.936 ``` :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_re_pred |> specificity(truth = class, estimate = .pred_class) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> .metric .estimator .estimate #> #> 1 specificity binary 0.865 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](images/confusion-matrix-specificity.png) ::: ::: ## Two class data These metrics assume that we know the threshold for converting "soft" probability predictions into "hard" class predictions. . . . Is a 50% threshold good? What happens if we say that we need to be 80% sure to declare an event? - sensitivity ⬇️, specificity ⬆️ . . . What happens for a 20% threshold? - sensitivity ⬆️, specificity ⬇️ ## Varying the threshold ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](figures/thresholds-1.svg) ::: ::: ## ROC curves ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} For an ROC (receiver operator characteristic) curve, we plot - the false positive rate (1 - specificity) on the x-axis - the true positive rate (sensitivity) on the y-axis with sensitivity and specificity calculated at all possible thresholds. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](figures/roc-curve-1-1.svg){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: :::notes ROC curves are insensitive to class imbalance. ::: ::: {.absolute bottom=0 left=0} [AML4TD](https://aml4td.org/chapters/cls-metrics.html#sec-roc) ::: ## ROC curves ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} We can use the area under the ROC curve as a classification metric: - ROC AUC = 1 💯 - ROC AUC = 1/2 😢 ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](figures/roc-curve-2-1.svg){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## ROC curves ![](hexes/yardstick.png){.absolute top=-20 right=0 width="64" height="74.24"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Assumes _first_ factor level is event; <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
